title: How to Connect Sales Orders and Purchase Orders for Better Inventory Decisions
summary: Learn the difference between a sales order vs. purchase order, and see how connecting them helps brands set better promise dates and make smarter reorders.
body_markdown:
Want to test drive the most customizable ERP platform in the market?


A sales order and a purchase order describe the same kind of transaction from opposite sides. The buyer commits to buy, and the seller commits to deliver.


Most explanations of sales orders vs. purchase orders stop there. But for brands that sell wholesale and direct-to-consumer — while also buying from their own suppliers — it’s important to understand how the two documents connect inside their systems.


Seeing SOs and POs as two halves of one inventory story helps a whole lot of things get easier, like promising delivery dates with confidence, sizing reorders around accurate demand, and keeping customers happy.


**What you’ll learn:**


-


The difference between sales orders and purchase orders


-


How purchase orders and sales orders connect inside a growing brand


-


The way you can use open purchase orders as sellable inventory


-


What happens when you connect sales orders and purchase orders with headless, composable ERP


## Sales Order vs. Purchase Order: The Quick Difference


A purchase order comes first. It’s a buyer’s commitment to buy, detailing exactly what they want.[A sales order is a seller’s commitment to deliver,](https://www.tailor.tech/resources/posts/understanding-sales-order-process-orders-pos-invoices-explained) putting fulfillment in motion.


Brands that sell to retailers and buy from suppliers write both. In fact, you might write both a sales order and a purchase order for the same product in the same week.


Here’s what this might look like in practice for a growing brand:


A boutique’s purchase order arrives and becomes your sales order (the same transaction seen from two sides). Direct-to-consumer (DTC) orders from Shopify, Amazon, and TikTok Shop skip over the PO step and turn into sales orders as soon as checkout goes through. Finally, you issue purchase orders to your manufacturers and suppliers, and their systems turn those POs into their sales orders.


If you’re on both sides of the table every day, the important thing to know is how your SOs and POs connect.


## How Purchase Orders and Sales Orders Connect Inside a Growing Brand


Sales orders capture demand, purchase orders bring in supply, and inventory is where they meet. A high-quality meeting point lets you sell with confidence and purchase with precision.


[Imagine a skincare brand sells its cleanser and serum on Shopify](https://www.tailor.tech/resources/posts/shopify-growing-pains) and Amazon, wholesales to ~40 boutiques, and buys from one contract manufacturer and one packaging supplier. Its holiday gift set (comprised of the cleanser, serum, a branded box, and an insert card) uses one sales order line to draw on four components — each bought using its own PO.


### Demand: Sales Orders From Every Channel


Sales orders come from more places than you might realize. Yet each one takes a share of the same inventory. The skincare brand from our example is managing demand via both wholesale commitments and DTC orders (which move more quickly than steady wholesale orders).


-


**Wholesale:** A boutique’s PO becomes a sales order. Larger accounts might send POs by Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) to automatically create the SO.


-


**DTC:** As soon as checkout clears, Shopify and Amazon orders turn into sales orders. If you’re running a promo, you might see hundreds of sales orders per day.


-


**Allocation:** Each SO reserves inventory when it’s created, changing what’s available for every other channel.


### Supply: Purchase Orders to Your Suppliers


Your brand answers demand with purchase orders — the skincare brand would send POs to the manufacturer and packaging supplier. Think of purchase orders as future inventory that you can plan around. Each PO comes with a timeline that affects what you can realistically promise.


-


**Lead times:** Different POs are going to have different lead times. Finished goods from the contract manufacturer might take eight weeks; the branded boxes and insert cards from the packaging supplier could take just three. But the timeline of the full gift set must be planned around its slowest component.


-


**Future inventory:** Open POs represent future inventory. Stock that’s been ordered, but hasn’t arrived, is still useful information.


-


**Receiving and matching:** After a shipment arrives, the PO, receipt, and supplier invoice are matched before the record goes to accounting.


### Where They Meet: One Inventory Picture


When SOs and POs share data, allocations and incoming stock appear side-by-side. Your team has visibility into exactly what’s sellable now, what’s arriving, and what needs to be reordered.


But when these two documents live in separate places, gaps show up right when your business is growing the fastest.


When both documents read from the same record, these gaps close. That shared record opens up useful possibilities.


## Open Purchase Orders as Sellable Inventory


Connected SOs and POs allow you to sell confidently against stock that’s still on the way and to buy with real demand in view, turning two documents into a growth lever.


### Selling Against Incoming Supply


When your sales system can see open purchase orders, you can promise against stock that’s still on the way:


-


Firm delivery dates for preorders and wholesale orders, backed by confirmed PO arrivals.


-


Planned backorders, matched to the open PO that will fill it.


-


Clear allocation calls when incoming stock can’t cover every channel.


### Buying From Actual Demand


When your purchase orders follow your sales orders, every reorder improves:


-


PO quantities based on current sales trends, not last quarter’s spreadsheet


-


Component orders timed to each supplier’s lead time


-


AI-suggested reorders that a person reviews and approves


### What Connected SO and PO Data Unlocks


After POs are matched to receipts and invoices, Tailor connects clean records to QuickBooks, Xero, or your preferred accounting software.


But all of this depends on what’s underneath: one record that every channel, supplier, and system can rely on.
